text: Cosmo Armstrong was the son of John Armstrong and was apprenticed in 1787 to John Gyde, a citizen and loriner. He was a pupil of Thomas Milton, the landscape engraver. He became a governor of the Society of Engravers and showed with the Associated Engravers in 1821. He engraved plates for editions of the British Poets, the British Classics and Shakespeare. He worked as an English line-engraver.

Ludovico Lana directed the Accademia Ducale of Modena and was mainly active there, where he died in 1646. He is said to have been born in Codigoro to a Ferrarese merchant whose family came from Brescia. He appears to have trained with Scarsellino in Ferrara. He then spent some time in Bologna, where he may have worked under or learned the style of Reni or Guercino. He painted in the Baroque style.

Willem van Nieulandt spent two thirds of his career in the Habsburg Netherlands and the rest in Italy and the Dutch Republic. He came from Antwerp. He is known for Italianate landscape paintings and prints, often real views or capricci of landscapes and buildings in or around Rome, enlivened by figures from his day or by biblical or mythological scenes. He was also a poet and playwright, and an engraver.

Alfred Ost's first drawings were realistic studies of animals and genre scenes. Then he turned to religious themes, transposed into a contemporary popular context. He became known as an animal painter and poster designer. His experiences in the war, made worse by bipolar disorder, brought dark colouring and pessimistic themes into his later art. He was a Belgian painter, watercolorist and political cartoonist. He died in Antwerp in 1945.

William Daniell travelled extensively in India with his uncle Thomas Daniell, and together they made Oriental Scenery, one of the finest illustrated works of the period. Later he went round the coastline of Britain painting watercolours for another ambitious book, A Voyage Round Great Britain. He specialised in landscape and marine art and made prints. His work was shown at the Royal Academy and the British Institution. He died in 1837.

Muirhead Bone became known for industrial and architectural subjects, and for his work as a war artist in both world wars. He belonged to the last generation of the Etching Revival. His early large, heavily worked architectural etchings fetched extremely high prices before the Wall Street crash of 1929 deflated the collectors' market. He was a Scottish etcher and watercolourist and was knighted. He died in 1953.

Cornelis Troost trained as an actor and married the actress Susanna Maria van der Duyn. In 1723 he became a pupil of Arnold Boonen and gave up the stage for painting. He is mainly remembered for scenes from the Amsterdam theatre, for which he also made decorations, and for daily life among the upper crust of Amsterdam. One of his earliest drawings, from 1708, shows Prince Eugene of Savoy. He died in 1750.

Samuel Prout largely invented the grand street scene in British watercolour, mostly with picturesque views of continental cities. In 1829 he became Painter in Water-Colours in Ordinary to King George IV, and afterwards to Queen Victoria. Ruskin, whose work often copied his, wrote that he sometimes tired of Turner but never of Prout. He was a master of watercolour architectural painting. He lived from 1783 to 1852.

Georges Clairin befriended the actress Sarah Bernhardt, and the two stayed friends for 50 years. He is best known for his informal portraits of her, often in costume. He was an Orientalist painter and illustrator, influenced by Eastern imagery and Moorish architecture. He visited North Africa many times, particularly Algeria, Morocco and Egypt. In Paris he led the life of a socialite. He lived from 1843 to 1919.

John William Edy worked for the publisher John Boydell in London, often anonymously. In the summer of 1800 he visited Norway on an assignment for Boydell with the landscape painter William Fearnside. They stayed from 31 July until the end of September. Edy made numerous drawings on the trip, among them views of Ny-Hellesund, where the two artists arrived. He is also known in Norway for drawings of Christiania. He lived from 1760 to 1820.

Born in Turin, Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier became known as a worker in Paris, where he died. He was a goldsmith, sculptor, painter, architect and furniture designer. His Italian origin and training probably account for the extravagance of his decorative style. He dealt with the Rococo in its most daring and flamboyant developments. Rarely did he leave a foot or two of surface undecorated. He lived from 1695 to 1750.

Léonard Gaultier, who sometimes signed himself Galter, was a French engraver born at Mainz about 1561. His style resembles that of Wierix and Crispyn van de Passe. His prints are cut entirely with the graver, with great precision but in a stiff, formal manner. He must have worked very hard, since the Abbé de Marolles owned over eight hundred prints by him, many after his own designs. He died in Paris in 1641.

Jiao Bingzhen came from Jining, Shandong, and became a painter and also an astronomer. He is one of the first Qing dynasty painters to blend traditional Chinese painting with Western culture. He is also among the more significant portrait and miniature painters of the early Qing. He was skilled at painting people, landscapes and buildings. He was active from 1689 to 1726.

Godfrey Kneller, born Gottfried Kniller in Germany, became the leading portraitist in England in the late Stuart and early Georgian eras. He served as court painter to successive monarchs, including Charles II and George I. He also painted scientists such as Isaac Newton, foreign monarchs like Louis XIV, and visitors to England. He was made a baronet. He lived from 1646 to 1723.

Nadar, born Gaspard-Félix Tournachon, worked as a photographer, caricaturist, journalist, novelist and balloonist. He argued for heavier-than-air flight. In 1858 he became the first person to take aerial photographs. Many of the great national collections hold his photographic portraits, and his son Paul continued the studio after his death. He lived from 1820 to 1910, and signed with the pseudonym Nadar.

Charles Demuth worked mainly in watercolor and turned to oils late in his career, developing a style called Precisionism. Ken Johnson wrote in The New York Times that few American watercolors are more beautiful than Demuth's. His flowers, fruit and vegetables combine exact botanical observation with loosely Cubist abstraction, and they have a magical liveliness. He was American. He lived from 1883 to 1935.

Truman Seymour combined a military career with painting. The son of a Methodist minister in Burlington, Vermont, he served in the Union Army in the Civil War and rose to major general. He was present at the Battle of Fort Sumter. At the Battle of Olustee, the only major battle fought in Florida, he commanded the Union troops. His pictures include a view of Fort Leavenworth. He lived from 1824 to 1891.

Ventura Álvarez Sala began at the local drawing school in Gijón and as an apprentice in the workshop of the decorative painter Dionisio Canal. In 1890 he moved to Madrid, where he supported himself by making charcoal sketches on demand. Later he studied with Manuel Ojeda and José Jiménez. He painted portraits and genre scenes, many with maritime subjects, and worked as an illustrator. He died in 1919.

François Nicolas Augustin Feyen added his mother's maiden name, Perrin, to Feyen so as to stand apart from his older brother Jacques-Eugène, who was already an established artist. Their father was a tax collector in Bey-sur-Seille. His first art lessons came from his brother. He worked as a painter, engraver and illustrator in France. He lived from 1826 to 1888.

Carlo Fontana came from near Como, in what is now the Swiss canton of Ticino. No proof exists that he belonged to the famous family of architects that included Domenico Fontana, though he is sometimes called his great-nephew. He worked in Rome and was partly responsible for the classicizing direction of Late Baroque Roman architecture. He lived from 1638 to 1714.

Charles Fremont Conner was self-taught and began his career as an industrial painter for the Hoosier Drill Company in Richmond, Indiana, where he painted decorations and small landscape scenes on farm machinery. He worked alongside artists such as Frank Girardin and Micajah Nordyke. He is counted among the most talented early Richmond artists and among the most important painters of the Richmond Group. He lived from 1857 to 1905.

Goethe's friends called Johann Heinrich Meyer Goethemeyer, because he was such a close associate of the poet. Meyer grew up in Stäfa, near Lake Zürich, the son of a merchant. He took his first drawing lessons at sixteen. He worked as a painter, engraver and art critic. He served as the second Director of the Weimar Princely Free Drawing School. He lived from 1760 to 1832.

Antonie Sminck Pitloo added an extra o to his surname because people in Italy often mistook him for an Italian. In Italian he is also known as Antonio van Pitloo. He came from Arnhem and studied painting first in Paris, then in Rome from 1811, where there was already an international artistic colony. A scholarship helped him. He died in 1837.

Martin Kober, of Polish descent, trained as a guild painter and travelled through Germany for three years as a journeyman. He worked as a portrait painter and court painter to several Central European monarchs, among them Stephen Báthory and Rudolf II. He was active mainly in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. His name has many spellings, such as Chober, Cober and Koeber. He died before 1598.

Vittore Carpaccio and Benedetto Rusconi were among the students of Lazzaro Bastiani. He came from Padua and was first recorded as a painter in Venice by 1460, in a payment for an altarpiece of San Samuele. A couple of years later he was paid at the same rate as Giovanni Bellini. By 1470 he belonged to the Scuola di San Girolamo in Venice. He died in 1512.

Bjarne Ness, the eldest of six siblings, grew up in Trondheim. He got his first professional drawing lessons at the Norwegian Institute of Technology with Harald Krohg Stabell. In 1923 he attended the railway school in Hamar. A year later he became a student at Axel Revold's painting school. He worked as a painter and illustrator. He died young, in 1927.

Gottlieb Bodmer first painted portraits under Stieler in Munich. In 1829 he lithographed the Madonna di San Sisto, after an engraving by F. Müller, and later two paintings after H. Hess. He is favourably known by these works. He visited Paris and then returned to Munich, where he died. He lived from 1804 to 1837.

Signe Scheel studied with Christian Krohg in Norway, with Karl Gussow in Berlin, and with Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret at the Académie Colarossi in Paris. She exhibited often at the Høstutstillingen. Her most famous work, The Lord's Servant, is in the National Museum of Art in Oslo. She came from Hamar and died in Oslo in 1942. A prize was later named for her.

Count Albert de Balleroy painted and etched, and also sat in parliament. He specialised in subjects related to hunting. His Le Cerf à l'hallali is in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Caen, and Le Débuché is at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. His large canvases often show packs of hounds. He lived from 1828 to 1872.

Mochizuki Gyokusen came from a samurai family in Kyoto and founded the Mochizuki school of painting in the early 1700s. He studied under the Tosa school master Tosa Mitsunari, and later under the Kano teacher Yamaguchi Sekkei. He began by drawing gold or silver patterns on lacquer seal cases, then developed a style of his own. He lived from 1692 to 1755.

Zacharie Heince, born in Paris, was a well known French painter and engraver of Swiss origin. He drew portraits of the plenipotentiaries negotiating the peace of Münster, which F. Bignon engraved in 33 plates plus a frontispiece, in 1648. He also drew the Illustrious Frenchmen painted in the gallery of the Palais Richelieu, in 27 engraved plates. He died in Paris in 1669.

Sir David Young Cameron painted, and with greater success etched, mostly townscapes and landscapes. He was a leading figure in the final decades of the Etching Revival. He was born in Glasgow, the son of the Rev. Robert Cameron of the United Presbyterian Church, and was one of five children. His sister Katharine was an artist too. He lived from 1865 to 1945.

Paris is where Wojciech Kossak came into the world, just before midnight on New Year's Eve 1856, and his twin brother Tadeusz, a freedom fighter, followed after midnight. Their father Juliusz Kossak was a painter, and the family produced many artists and writers. Wojciech's daughters Maria Pawlikowska-Jasnorzewska and Magdalena Samozwaniec became writers, and his son Jerzy a painter. He died in 1942.

Peter Christian Thamsen Skovgaard, known as P C Skovgaard, is considered one of the leading landscape painters of the 19th century. He was a Danish national romantic and one of the main figures of the Golden Age of Danish Painting. He is especially known for large portrayals of the Danish landscape. Among his early pictures is a portrait of the painter J Th Lundbye. He lived from 1817 to 1875.

Domenico Maria Fratta studied under Giovanni Maria Viani, Carlo Rambaldi and Donato Creti in his native Bologna. Then he gave up painting and devoted himself entirely to engraving, which brought him widespread fame. He became a member of the Accademia Clementina. He worked as a painter and engraver in Bologna. He lived from 1696 to 1763.

Enoch Wood Perry Jr. was known for portraits and landscapes. He came from Boston and lived in Philadelphia, New Orleans, northern California, Hawaii and New York City. His father was Enoch Wood Perry and his mother Hannah Knapp Dole. Among his pictures are Talking It Over and The True American. He lived from 1831 to 1915.

Oskar Marmorek came from Pieskowa Skała in Galicia, the eldest of five children in a family that moved several times. He worked as an architect and was a Zionist. His plans include the site plan of Venice in Vienna, from 1895, and the English garden for an international exhibition two years later. He lived from 1863 to 1909.

William Barraud painted animals and illustrated. He collaborated with his brother Henry on many works. He was one of 17 children, born in Lambeth, London, to a clerk in the Custom House. His paternal grandfather was an eminent chronometer maker in Cornhill. He lived from 1810 to 1850.

Daniel Huntington belonged to the Hudson River School and later became a prominent portrait painter. He came from New York City, the son of Benjamin Huntington Jr. His grandfather was a delegate to the Second Continental Congress. He lived from 1816 to 1906.

Luc-Olivier Merson grew up in an artistic household in Paris, the son of a painter and art critic. He studied under Gustave Chassevent at the École de Dessin and then Isidore Pils at the École des Beaux-Arts. He worked as an academic painter and illustrator. He also designed postage stamps and currency. He lived from 1846 to 1920.

Léon Lhermitte's father, a schoolteacher, noticed his talent for drawing and encouraged him. He grew up in Mont-Saint-Père in Picardy in a cultivated but modest family. He worked as a naturalist painter and etcher, and his main subject was rural scenes of peasants at work. He lived from 1844 to 1925.
